newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Drought cuts Tanzania tea production by a quarter.
newsitem.headline: Drought cuts Tanzania tea production by a quarter.

text.p: Drought in East Africa will cause a 25 percent loss in Tanzanian tea production in the 1996/97 season, a senior tea industry official said on Friday.
"Our projection for 1996/97 is because of the effect of the drought (affecting) 20 to 25 percent of the whole country.

"It will be down by almost 40 percent for Usumbaras (northern tea region)," said Salum Mijinga, Managing Director of the state-run Tanzania Tea Authority (TTA). The Usambara teas are named after the mountain range on which they grown.

Production of tea, Tanzania's third biggest agricultural export earner after coffee and cotton, was expected to be in the range of 18 million kg (39.69 million lb) worth about $21 million at current market prices, Mijinga told Reuters.
This compared with a production of 22 million kg (48.51 million lb) and worth $20 million in 1995/96. The disparity in earnings was due to falling prices on the world market in 1995/96.
"Prices (1995/96) were the lowest in 40 years -- about 90 cents per kilogram," Mijinga said. "This year they started picking up around $1.20 as an average at the Mombasa auctions."
He attributed this year's price hike to the drought saying production had also fallen in neighbouring Kenya, Africa's biggest tea producing country.

Tanzania had a good season in 1994/95 when production reached 25,271,529 kg of tea worth a record $26.2 million. Ten years ago (1986/87) 14.06 million kgs were produced earning $24.5 million. The TTA crop season matches the financial year (July/June).

Mijinga said the Usumbara teas grown in northern Tanga region would be hardest hit by the drought. They normally account for 30 percent of total Tanzanian tea production and are grown in three districts, Muheza, Karogwe and Lushoto.
Tanzania's tea industry dates to 1902 when the first crop was planted by German colonial settlers in northern Tanga.
About 80 percent of annual production is exported, mainly to Middle East countries, but also to Sudan, Pakistan and Europe. The remaining 20 percent is used for domestic consumption.

Green tea is produced by smallholders as well as large tea estates. Mijinga said there was widespread scope for expansion of the local tea industry with up to 20,000 hectares (49,420 acres) of land available for additional production.

Some 20,000 hectares is currently under production, half of which is run by small holders, 30 percent private estates, 10 percent TTA estates and 10 percent public sector estates. --Nairobi Newsroom ++254-2 330-261.
